name: CPAP (sleep apnea)

image.caption: CPAP continuous positive airway pressure mask installed

lead: CPAP delivers air at constant pressure through a mask to keep your airway open during sleep. It is described as the most effective treatment for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea. In appearance communities, it is discussed for the fresher, less puffy look that comes with restored sleep.

Pressurised air splints the upper airway open, which eliminates obstructive apneas in most people who use it as directed, so sleep is no longer repeatedly broken. Better sleep is what users connect to less facial puffiness. In people with sleep apnea it lowers overall cardiovascular death risk; appearance outcomes have not been tested in the sources reviewed.

paras: CPAP is a prescription device used nightly with a nasal, full-face or hybrid mask after a sleep study diagnoses apnea. Users adjust mask type and fit with their provider. Sleep quality often changes within days to weeks of consistent use.

Adherence is a major issue: about 8% stop after the first night and more than half within a year. Reported side effects include discomfort, congestion, bloating, claustrophobia and mask leaks. It is a prescription medical device and needs a diagnosis.

web.title: Reversal of obstructive sleep apnoea by continuous positive airway pressure applied through the nares

angle.text: CPAP keeps the airway open at night so sleep is no longer repeatedly broken, and online discussion links that restored sleep with less facial puffiness and a fresher look. It is the standard treatment for moderate to severe sleep apnea; appearance outcomes were not studied in the sources reviewed.

lead: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) delivers air at a steady, slightly raised pressure through a mask to keep the upper airway open during sleep.  For people with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), it is the route to unbroken, properly oxygenated sleep, and in looksmaxxing circles that matters for looks because sleep is the foundation that training, recovery, skin and day-to-day energy are built on. Lifters on T Nation describe the first nights on CPAP as a turning point in how rested and trainable they feel. [1][2]

The adult machine was invented by the Australian physician Colin Sullivan, who built it in 1980 at Royal Prince Alfred Hospital in Sydney and published the design in The Lancet in 1981; Respironics began selling one of the first commercial adult units in 1985. [3][4] CPAP is described as the most effective treatment for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea, and in people with sleep apnea it lowers overall risk of cardiovascular death.

In looksmaxxing communities the device comes up in three ways: as a sleep-quality tool that members connect to a fresher face and better training; as one option set beside mandibular advancement devices, myofunctional therapy and jaw surgery when an airway is narrow; and as a topic inside jaw-surgery (bimaxillary or maxillomandibular advancement) discussions, where a recessed jaw is described as both a breathing and an aesthetic matter. [5][6][7] Published trials compare CPAP with the alternatives on blood pressure, cardiovascular and cognitive outcomes; no appearance study of CPAP itself has been located. [8][9][10][11]
infobox: Nasal pillows, nasal mask, full-face, hybrid
Moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea
Mandibular advancement devices, myofunctional therapy, jaw surgery, weight loss [12][16]
About 8% stop after night one; over half within a year

paras: CPAP uses a motor that pressurises room-temperature air and sends it along a hose to a mask or nasal interface; the constant pressure acts as an air splint that keeps the airway open on both inhalation and exhalation.  Many units add a heated humidifier and smartphone apps that report nightly data such as mask leak and hours of use.

Interfaces include nasal pillows that sit at the base of the nostrils, nasal masks, full-face masks that cover nose and mouth (used for mouth breathers and oral leaks), and hybrid masks that combine a mouth portion with a nasal cushion.  Surgical tape over the lips or a chin strap is sometimes used to limit mouth leaks.  CPAP is distinct from the related PEEP technique used in ventilators, which applies pressure only at the end of exhalation.

Outside sleep apnea, CPAP is used in neonatal intensive care for infant respiratory distress syndrome, a use developed at the University of California, San Francisco, in 1971, and for acute heart failure and some other respiratory conditions.

Obstructive sleep apnea involves repeated partial or complete collapse of the upper airway during sleep. Excessive daytime sleepiness is the hallmark, along with loud snoring, gasping, restless sleep, morning headaches, concentration problems and mood changes. [12] Severity is graded by the apnea-hypopnea index (events per hour): under 5 is normal in adults, 5 to 15 mild, 15 to 30 moderate and 30 or more severe. [12] Diagnosis is by overnight polysomnography or home sleep testing. [12]

Reference works list obesity (fat around the neck narrows the airway), male sex, age, alcohol and sedatives, smoking and nasal obstruction among risk factors, along with craniofacial anatomy: a small or receded lower jaw, a narrow upper jaw and a displaced tongue base can narrow the airway. [12] This anatomical link is why apnea is discussed in jaw-surgery threads on looksmax.org, where members describe a recessed chin both as an aesthetic issue and a breathing one. [5][6] In children, enlarged tonsils and adenoids are a common cause, and a 2024 meta-analysis of 35 studies tied tonsillar hypertrophy, adenoid hypertrophy, respiratory infection, obesity and family history to paediatric OSA. [12][13]

sections.h: How people use it for looks
paras: Members of looksmaxxing communities connect untreated sleep apnea with tired eyes, puffiness and low energy, and connect treatment with a fresher look and better training sessions. Lifters on T Nation write of falling asleep at the wheel before diagnosis and of a large difference once they started CPAP; one forum user described a first great night of sleep in a long time after getting a machine. [1][2][14]

The chain people describe is sleep first, appearance second: unbroken, oxygenated sleep supports recovery from training, appetite and energy regulation, and a rested face. Proponents present CPAP as the foundation under other efforts rather than a cosmetic product in itself. These accounts come from users; no trial has measured facial appearance after CPAP.

Apnea also appears in jaw-surgery discussion on looksmax.org, where a recessed chin or narrow airway is described as both a breathing and an aesthetic issue, and members discuss whether insurance covers jaw surgery when it addresses apnea. [5][6][7] Members also discuss neck training in relation to apnea. [15] Some threads describe disappointing outcomes after jaw advancement done for sleep apnea, with posters describing profile changes and persistent breathing problems. [5]

Mandibular advancement devices are custom mouthpieces that move the lower jaw forward. Professional societies recommend oral appliances for people with OSA who cannot tolerate CPAP or prefer another option, and they are generally described as more effective for mild to moderate than for severe apnea; common side effects include dry mouth, tooth and jaw discomfort, and long-term changes in how the teeth meet. [16] A 2024 randomized equivalence trial compared mandibular advancement devices with CPAP for blood pressure reduction, and a randomized trial in severe apnea compared the two on other outcomes. [8][9]

Orofacial myofunctional therapy consists of tongue and oropharyngeal exercises. A 2024 meta-analysis of seven randomized trials (310 patients) reported improvements in apnea-hypopnea index, sleepiness and sleep-related quality of life, and a 2025 network meta-analysis of 15 trials found improved sleepiness and sleep quality scores, no statistically significant change in AHI overall, and a larger AHI reduction when therapy was combined with CPAP. [17][18]

Maxillomandibular advancement moves both jaws forward and is described as one of the most effective surgical options for sleep apnea, usually after other treatments have been tried; recovery is longer than for other airway surgeries because the facial bones must heal in their new positions. [7] Weight loss is a standard recommendation where obesity is present, and the FDA approved tirzepatide for OSA in adults with obesity in December 2024. [12] In children, a 2023 meta-analysis of mostly uncontrolled studies found that rapid maxillary expansion and mandibular advancement appliances improved apnea indices, while noting the low quality of the evidence. [19]

CPAP eliminates obstructive apneas in most people who use it as recommended.  Adherence is the main limiting factor: about 8% quit after the first night and more than half within the first year, because it must be used for all sleep including naps and travel, and pressure setting often takes trial and error.  People with moderate to severe OSA often have anxiety or depression, which can make consistent use harder, and a 2020 Cochrane review found educational and supportive interventions can improve use.  A review of predictors of adherence summarises factors associated with continued use. [20] Sullivan's first report in 1981 described five people with severe apnea who slept through the night at pressures of 4.5 to 10 cm of water. [4]

Users may report discomfort, nasal congestion, bloating and flatulence, claustrophobia, mask leaks and mouth leaks.  Contraindications listed include inability to protect the airway, facial trauma or burns, and recent facial or upper-digestive surgery.  A 2024 randomized trial examined how CPAP, mandibular advancement devices and myofunctional therapy affect the temporomandibular joint. [21]

Around 2010 Philips Respironics added polyurethane foam to some devices to reduce noise; the foam could degrade in heat and humidity and release particles and chemicals including formaldehyde. [22] Philips recalled the affected machines in 2021; reports say up to 15 million devices were involved, and the company later settled lawsuits and operates under an FDA and Department of Justice consent decree limiting new US sales. [22] In 2024 a Hacker News thread discussed the FDA report attributing 561 deaths to the recalled machines. [23]

CPAP is prescribed after a sleep study and typically supplied through a medical-equipment provider. Respironics, founded in 1976, received FDA clearance for its CPAP system in 1984 and was acquired by Philips in 2008 for about 5.1 billion dollars. [22] ResMed, founded by Peter Farrell in Australia in 1989 and headquartered in San Diego since 1994, is the other major maker and reported revenue of 4.7 billion dollars in fiscal 2024. [24]

A 1994 case series of seven patients with refractory partial epilepsy and sleep apnea reported reduced seizure frequency in six after treating apnea, including four of five using CPAP. [25] The SAVE randomized trial enrolled 2717 adults aged 45 to 75 with moderate-to-severe apnea and coronary or cerebrovascular disease, after a sham-CPAP run-in, and tested CPAP plus usual care for preventing cardiovascular events. [10] The RICCADSA trial examined positive airway pressure in coronary artery disease patients with non-sleepy apnea. [26] A 2023 JAMA individual-participant meta-analysis of SAVE, ISAACC and RICCADSA examined how adherence to CPAP relates to recurrent cardiovascular events. [27] A 2025 randomized trial examined CPAP effects on neuroimaging biomarkers and cognition. [11] Trials comparing CPAP with mandibular advancement and myofunctional therapy are described above. [8][9][21][18][17] No studies found examining CPAP for facial puffiness or appearance.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, sleep apnea is discussed mostly in the context of jaw surgery and airway size, while on T Nation lifters describe CPAP in terms of energy and training. [1][5]
